title: Schroeder's Conjecture (Conjecture 2)
statement_text: Let $G$ be a graph of genus $g$. Then $c(G) \leq g + 3$.
context_text: Schroeder proved that $c(G) \leq \lfloor \frac{3}{2}g \rfloor + 3$ for graphs of genus $g$ and conjectured the bound can be tightened. The conjecture holds for $g=1$ (the torus), but no toroidal graph with cop number 4 is known. Most researchers believe the conjectured bound is tight up to a constant, but no evidence supports this.
paper_contribution: Establishes the lower bound $c(g) \geq g^{1/2 - o(1)}$ using random-graph results of Bollobás, Kun, and Leader, and proposes the stronger Conjecture 8 that $c(g) = g^{1/2+o(1)}$, suggesting Schroeder's linear upper bound is far from tight.
paper_title: Notes on Cops and Robber game on graphs

title: Conjecture 8
statement_text: $c(g) = g^{\frac{1}{2}+o(1)}$ and $\widetilde c(g) = g^{\frac{1}{2}+o(1)}$. In other words, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $g_0$ such that for every $g \geq g_0$, $$g^{\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon} < c(g) < g^{\frac{1}{2}+\varepsilon}$$ and $$g^{\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon} < \widetilde c(g) < g^{\frac{1}{2}+\varepsilon}.$$
context_text: In the Cops and Robber game on a graph, $k$ cops and then a robber choose vertices, and then alternately the cops (each moving along an edge or staying) and the robber move, with full information; the cop number $c(G)$ is the least $k$ for which the cops can always catch the robber. Here $c(g)=\max\{c(G) : g(G)\le g\}$ and $\widetilde c(g)=\max\{c(G) : \widetilde g(G)\le g\}$, where $g(G)$ is the (orientable) genus of $G$ and $\widetilde g(G)$ its nonorientable genus (crosscap number). Planar graphs have cop number at most $3$; guarding a shortest homologically non-trivial cycle with two cops gives $c(G)\le 2g+3$, and Schröder proved $c(G)\le\frac{3}{2}g+3$ for graphs of genus $g$ and conjectured $c(G)\le g+3$; most people believe Schröder's bound is tight up to a constant, but the author notes there is no evidence for this. Incidence graphs of projective planes give $c(g)=\Omega(g^{1/3})$, and random graphs $G(n,p)$ with $p=\frac{5}{2}\log(n)/n$ (using the Bollobás–Kun–Leader bounds on their cop number) give, for every $\varepsilon>0$ and large $g$, graphs of genus $g$ with $g^{1/2-\varepsilon}\le c(G)\le g^{1/2+\varepsilon}$, so $c(g)\ge g^{\frac{1}{2}(1-o(1))}$. The author (Mohar, 2009) conjectures that this is the true order, i.e. a much stronger upper bound than Schröder's; the conjecture was unchallenged when the note was written.

title: Question (Riemannian surfaces): cop number bounded by genus
statement_text: Is the cop number of Riemannian surfaces bounded in terms of the genus?
context_text: The author proposes a Cops and Robber game on a Riemannian surface $S$: $k$ cops and a robber are placed on $S$, all move with velocity at most $1$ (during time $t$ each player moves along a path of length at most $t$), the players know each other's positions at all times, and the robber is caught when some cop gets at distance less than $\frac{1}{2}$ from him; the cop number of $S$ is the least $k$ for which the cops can always catch the robber. There are two versions: a continuous one where all players move continuously (the author notes that what a strategy means needs justification, perhaps as a limit of the discrete game when time units tend to $0$), and a discrete one where the cops move during the day (one time unit) while the robber sleeps, then guard their neighbourhood up to distance $\frac{1}{2}$ during the night, when the robber moves. The geodesic path lemma carries over: one cop can guard a geodesic path $I$ (after reaching it and spending time equal to its length to adjust). This motivates the analogy with graphs, where the cop number of a graph of genus $g$ is at most $\frac{3}{2}g+3$ (Schröder) and is conjectured by the author to be $g^{1/2+o(1)}$ in the worst case. The question asks whether there is a bound on the cop number of a Riemannian surface depending only on its topological genus.
